newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya tightens pre-poll security after blast.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya tightens pre-poll security after blast.

text.p: Security officials in Chechnya said on Friday they were taking special measures to prevent any violence marring Monday's elections in the independence-seeking Russian region.

But the local interior minister said disruption to the polls could not be ruled out and, underlining the tensions in the turbulent Caucasian territory, an explosion killed five rail workers on a railway track in neighbouring Dagestan.
Security services were trying to establish the cause of the blast.
Police in Chechnya went on alert and the rebel authorities pledged to provide armed guards for each of more than 100 international observers arriving to monitor the vote.
"From today Interior Ministry personnel have been put on heightened alert," local Interior Minister Kazbek Makhashev told reporters in Grozny, the Chechen capital.
"It is difficult to exclude provocations by forces who want to destabilise the situation in the republic," he added.

Two Russian Orthodox priests, kidnapped two weeks ago in Chechnya, were freed on Friday. Father Yevfimy and his assistant Alexei said they had not been ill-treated but had little idea where they had been, who seized them or why they were released.

The kidnapping, coming after the killing of six foreign Red Cross workers and the death of several ethnic Russians, had further stoked tensions in the mainly Moslem region ahead of the presidential and parliamentary elections.
A senior official insisted that the abduction had been the work of "criminals" and had no political motive.

Russia sent troops into Chechnya in 1994 to crush its independence drive but pulled them out less than two years later after humiliating defeats, leaving the oil-rich region with its de facto sovereignty intact.

All 16 of the presidenital candidates support an independent Chechnya and most say Russia is trying to sabotage the vote by provoking crimes against civilians and objecting to voting rules for refugees.
Last-ditch efforts to find a common position and unite round one candidate apparently failed.
"There is now absolutely no chance of a common candidate," Mayerbek Vachagayev, top aide to front-runner Aslan Maskhadov, a former rebel chief commander, told Reuters.
He said acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev had suggested fielding a common candidate only because he had little chance of winning and not from a desire to preserve unity.
He said a survey conducted by Maskhadov's camp among several hundred voters in Grozny and in rural areas over the last three days suggested that 62 percent of voters were likely to support Maskhadov.
Yandarbiyev, former field commander Shamil Basayev and wartime propaganda chief Movladi Udugov each had 11 to 15 percent of the vote, he said.
Maskhadov, seen by many as the most moderate candidate, needs to clear the 50 percent barrier to avoid a runoff with the second-place vote-getter two weeks later.
A Reuter straw poll of 150 likely Grozny voters taken Wednesday and Thursday gave him about 57 percent of the vote.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which has helped to organise the elections, said 75 observers would work under its auspices while a further 40, including Russians, will work independently.
Tim Guldimann, the Swiss diplomat in charge of the OSCE mission in Grozny, said it would spend more than $600,000 to assist the Chechen government in running the vote.
